notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material from Guzik (Enduring Word), Precept Austin and the Pulpit Commentary, and some notes from the StudyLight compilations (Gill, Ellicott, Barnes, Henry, Lange and others). I ran out of search and page-reading capacity before I could reach the Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan, Lutheran or Pentecostal sites, or bibleodyssey. Those sections are therefore missing, not empty because nothing exists.

One sourcing caveat: I read the full Enduring Word, Precept Austin and Pulpit pages, but the tool didn't return them in a form I can tag with exact sentences. Notes from those pages have their URL in brackets after them. Notes that also appeared in search snippets have inline citations.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** The Pulpit Commentary says Agrippa leads only because Festus allows it. It reads Paul's raised hand as a speaker's opening gesture, made more striking by the chains on his arms. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Precept Austin notes this wasn't really a trial with charges. Festus's problem was that he had to invent charges to send to Nero with Paul.  Guzik points out Agrippa's family history: his great-grandfather tried to kill the infant Jesus, his grandfather beheaded John the Baptist, and his father killed James. 

**v. 2:** Guzik gives two reasons Paul was glad: high officials would weigh his case, and he could preach to kings.  He links this to the promise in Acts 9:15. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-26/] Precept Austin warns against reading "fortunate" as luck: Paul was there by God's providence and saw it as a blessing.

**v. 3:** McGee says Paul was glad to address someone who knew the Law of Moses and Jewish background.  The Pulpit notes that the word for "acquainted/expert" appears only here in the New Testament. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html]

**vv. 4–5:** Guzik notes that Paul was born in Tarsus but moved to Jerusalem young, and was known as a faithful Jew among the strictest party. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-26/] The Pulpit says Paul doesn't deny he is still a Pharisee. He tries to win over whatever goodwill the Jews still had for him. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html]

**vv. 6–7:** The Pulpit takes "the hope" as the hope of Christ's kingdom, which includes the resurrection. On this view Paul is the true Jew and his Sadducee accusers are the ones departing from it. It takes "night and day" as a reference to temple worship. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Guzik says Paul's faith in Jesus grew out of his trust in God's promise. 

**v. 8:** Wiersbe notes that "you" is plural, so Paul was addressing the whole room, including Greeks, Romans and Sadducees who rejected resurrection.  Guzik says Agrippa, as an expert in Jewish matters, should have understood belief in resurrection. 

**v. 9:** The Pulpit thinks Paul gently excuses his hearers' unbelief by admitting he once shared it. By saying "Jesus of Nazareth" he identifies himself with the Nazarenes. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Precept Austin says attacks on Christians were in the end attacks on Jesus himself. 

**v. 10:** Guzik says "cast my vote" suggests Paul sat on the Sanhedrin.  He adds a guess that Paul was therefore once married. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-26/] The Pulpit agrees that Paul voted in the Sanhedrin. It rejects Meyer's view that the phrase only means he approved. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html]

**v. 11:** The Pulpit says "tried to make them blaspheme" doesn't mean he always succeeded. It cites Pliny's remark that true Christians can't be forced to curse Christ. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Guzik suggests forcing others to blaspheme may have weighed most on Paul's conscience. 

**vv. 12–13:** Guzik notes that Paul's mission had the backing of the same leaders now accusing him. He saw the light literally before he saw it figuratively.  Precept Austin says the light outshone the sun at its brightest point, noon. 

**v. 14:** The Pulpit says "in Hebrew" is a new detail. It stresses that Paul is a thorough Jew and that Christianity fits Israel's life. "Kick against the goads" was a Greek proverb, found in Euripides and others, about pointless resistance to a stronger power. Paul should give in to God's constraining grace. The writer doubts the Jews used this proverb. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Guzik draws three points: Jesus' personal appeal, the target of the persecution ("Me"), and its folly ("Why"). 

**v. 15:** Guzik says Paul realised at once that Jesus was alive and reigning. He had to repent of misguided religious zeal rather than of immorality. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-26/]

**v. 16:** The Pulpit thinks Paul merges several messages into one: the road, Ananias, and a later trance. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Guzik reads "stand up" as "come now, let's be going."  The NET note links the commission to Acts 1:8.  Larkin says the word for "servant" means Paul must do exactly what his master says. 

**vv. 17–18:** Guzik lists four results of opened eyes: darkness to light, Satan to God, forgiveness, and an inheritance.  He takes "sanctified by faith" to mean set apart by trusting Jesus, not by works. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-26/] He also sees it as an invitation aimed at Agrippa. 

**v. 19:** The Pulpit says the wording is skilful, as if Paul were asking how anyone could blame him for obeying. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Wiersbe says the fact that Paul kept going proved his conversion was real. 

**v. 20:** Guzik treats "repent" and "turn" as two sides of one act, with deeds confirming that repentance is real. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-26/] The Pulpit explains why "all Judea" doesn't contradict Galatians 1:22. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html]

**v. 21:** Guzik says he was seized for taking the gospel to Gentiles, not for politics or defiling the temple. 

**v. 22:** Guzik notes that God's help gave Paul chances to speak, not release.  The Pulpit takes "I stand" as standing firm, not crushed by his enemies. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html]

**v. 23:** Guzik sums up Paul's preaching as Christ's death, resurrection, and the message to all nations.  The Pulpit, following Chrysostom, ties "first" to the resurrection, as in Colossians 1:18, and stresses fulfilled prophecy as evidence. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html]

**v. 24:** The Pulpit says Festus lacked spiritual discernment and that "madness" is a medical term. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Butler puts it this way: "The problem, however, was not the mentality of Paul, but the spirituality of Festus."

**v. 25:** The Pulpit says "soberness" is the opposite of the madness Festus charged. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Guzik says God may act above reason but never against it. 

**v. 26:** The Pulpit thinks Agrippa's manner showed he had been moved. Paul is a prisoner, but God's word isn't bound. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-26.html] Guzik says the events were open and public. 

**v. 27:** Guzik sees strategy here: believing the prophets should lead to believing in Jesus.  Kelly says Agrippa couldn't avoid admitting some impression, but this doesn't mean he believed. 

**v. 28:** The NET note calls Agrippa's question "probably a ploy on Agrippa's part to deflect Paul from his call for a decision". Constable says it doesn't mean he was close to converting.  Barnes takes the opposite view: he was nearly convinced. 

**v. 29:** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says Paul longed for everyone's salvation, however close or far they were.  Lange notes that "except these chains" points to the chain tying him to a soldier. 

**vv. 30–32:** Wiersbe says the king closed the hearing to escape the challenge.  Henry records a view that they kept Paul in custody so as not to offend the Jews. He comments that almost being persuaded was no better than not being persuaded at all.  Guzik sees the appeal to Caesar as serving God's plan to get Paul to Rome. 

## 2. Where traditions differ

- **v. 28, how to translate it.** The King James "almost" goes back to Chrysostom, Beza and Luther. The Pulpit calls the phrase "obscure."  On the other side, Calvin and others took it as "in a little time you will persuade me."  The Anglican Ellicott (labelled Arminian on StudyLight) drops "almost."  Lange reads Agrippa's reply as mocking. 
- **v. 28, how people come to faith.** *Contending for the Faith*, from the Church of Christ (Restorationist) tradition, stresses that Paul did the persuading. It criticises the sinner's prayer, prayer benches and "praying through." 
- **v. 20, repentance.** A note on Precept Austin with a Reformed slant says no one can repent unless God grants it.  I didn't find the Wesleyan or Lutheran side of this debate.

## 3. Other views

- **Modern scholarship:** Only the NET notes quoted on Precept Austin (vv. 16 and 28 above). Precept Austin also says the chapter is likely a summary of Paul's speech. 
- **Catholic, Orthodox, and popular modern teaching:** I didn't get to these.
